newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania's new leader wins quick backing from West.
newsitem.headline: Romania's new leader wins quick backing from West.

text.p: Romania's president-elect Emil Constantinescu on Monday pledged a new era of reforms and won Western backing to guide the country towards NATO and European Union membership.

After his victory over ex-communists, widely hailed as a new revolution seven years after eastern Europe's bloodiest uprising, Constantinescu assured voters he would fulfil campaign pledges to speed reforms and boost living standards.
That meant opening up capital markets, lifting restrictions on currency markets and ending foreign investment barriers to help raise Romanians from poverty level wages of $100 a month.

"I am convinced we will be able to make the necessary effort," he said. "We will succeed if we do away with incompetence and theft and if the austerity programme starts with austerity for the people at the top."
With 80 percent of the vote from Sunday's poll counted, Constantinescu held a 55 percent to 45 percent lead over Ion Iliescu, Romania's leader since its bloody upheaval in 1989.
Exit polls had given him a seven or eight point edge over the ex-communist, belying forecasts of a tight finish.

Constantinescu is to name a new government within days drawing heavily on his Democratic Convention (CDR), which started the big political changes earlier this month by throwing Iliescu's leftists out of government.
The Convention campaigned on fulfilling a "Contract with Romania" calling for tax cuts, improved benefits and liberalisation of markets within 200 days.
Encouragement was swift in coming from the West.
French President Jacques Chirac, on a visit to Japan, said Constantinescu's victory demonstrated "the openness of the Romanian people and its aspirations towards Europe".
"I am very pleased at the chance to work together to strengthen cooperation between France and Romania and to achieve an expanded Europe," Chirac said in a message.

German Finance Minister Theo Waigel, speaking as head of the conservative Bavarian Christian Social Union, said Constantinescu's pledges of reform "will significantly ease Romania's way into European and Atlantic structures".
"Now the spirit of freeedom has firmly triumphed in Romania too," he said. Constantinescu himself spoke of a positive response in Washington to the political changes.
On Bucharest streets, where tens of thousands of revellers celebrated the election outcome well into the night, students flashed victory signs at each other on their way to classes.
People generally expressed delight at the prospect of real change seven years after dictator Nicolae Ceausescu's execution but were all too aware of the difficulties ahead.
"There is a lot of hard work to be done. So many things to put right, especially in the economy," said Costica Nitu, 60. "It will probably not affect me so much at my stage in life."
Constantinescu told supporters Romania would "become once again the dignified and prosperous country we all wanted".
For Constantinescu, 57 on Tuesday, the victory was the final chapter in a revolution whose fruits opposition figures long argued were stolen from them by ex-communists.
Bucharest newspapers also greeted the outcome as the logical conclusion of a revolution launched seven years ago and whose goals were unfulfilled.
"The revolution of November 17, 1996," wrote commentator Ion Christoiu in the daily Evenimentul Zilei. "Emil is president, Romania rid of Iliescu," was the headline in Ziua.
